records.table: Jim Beam White Label is the Kentucky straight bourbon from Clermont, four years in new charred oak and bottled at 80 proof. Expect vanilla, caramel and oak with a little spice: a plain bourbon to taste the others against, and an easy highball.
records.story: As the brand tells it, the Beam family sold its first whiskey in Kentucky in 1795, a year that is the family's claim for its line rather than for this label, and its bourbon was sold for decades under the name Old Tub. James B. Beam (1864 to 1947) took charge of the family distillery in the 1890s, and Prohibition closed it in 1920. After repeal he rebuilt at Clermont with friends and family, and the first batch was ready in 1935. The rights to Old Tub had been lost, and in 1943 the bourbon took his own name, Jim Beam. The family tells of him carrying a jug of the house yeast home at weekends to keep it safe, and the house says it has used that strain since repeal. In 2014 Suntory of Japan bought Beam Inc., the company that then made it. For a bartender the White Label is the baseline: learn its vanilla, caramel and gentle spice, and every other bourbon on the back bar is tasted against it.

records.story: The distillery on the Kentucky River at Frankfort takes its name, by its own account, from the ancient traces that migrating buffalo wore through the wilderness to a crossing of the river there. A distillery called O.F.C. stood on the site by 1870. In 1878 it was bought by a St. Louis whiskey merchant, and from 1904 it carried his name as the George T. Stagg Distillery. Through Prohibition it kept working under a special government licence to bottle whiskey for medicinal use, one of a handful so permitted, and after repeal a metal-clad warehouse rose there that later housed Blanton's, first released in 1984 as a single barrel bourbon. The Sazerac Company bought the distillery in 1992, and in 1999 renamed it Buffalo Trace; a bourbon of the same name followed that year, made to its Mash Bill No. 1. For a bartender it is the everyday bottle of the distillery behind Weller, Blanton's and the Antique Collection: taste it first, and the rest of the family makes sense.

records.table: Wild Turkey 101 is the Kentucky straight bourbon from Lawrenceburg, bottled at 101 proof from barrels with a deep alligator char. Vanilla, toffee, baking spice and orange peel: the bourbon to reach for when a drink must stand up to citrus or vermouth.
records.story: Wild Turkey began as a merchant's label rather than a distillery. Austin, Nichols, a New York firm of merchants, bought its bourbon from Kentucky distilleries, the Ripy family's at Lawrenceburg among them. The name comes, the story goes, from a turkey hunt in 1940, when an executive of the firm took warehouse samples along, and his friends asked a year later for more of that wild turkey bourbon; some accounts put the hunt a few years earlier. By most accounts Austin, Nichols was bottling it under that name by 1942. In 1971 the firm bought the Lawrenceburg distillery, known then as the Boulevard Distillery, and renamed it for the label. Pernod Ricard bought the distillery and the brand in 1980, and the Campari Group bought both in 2009, bringing a new distillery on the site into use in 2011. A father and son, both master distillers there across decades, shaped its style. At 101 proof, from barrels filled at a low proof so that less water goes in at bottling, it is the bar's bourbon for a drink that has to hold its own.

records.story: A distillery stood on Glenn's Creek near Versailles by about 1812, built by the Pepper family, and whiskey was made there through much of the century. In 1878 the Peppers sold the property to the partnership of Labrot & Graham, whose name it took. Brown-Forman bought the distillery in 1941 and ran it until 1968, when it closed, and the land went back to farming. In the early 1990s Brown-Forman bought it back, restored the stone buildings and put in copper pot stills, and in 1996 it released Woodford Reserve, its bourbon from the old site. The distillery itself took the Woodford Reserve name only in 2003. Distiller's Select marries their triple distilled whiskey with column still whiskey from Brown-Forman's Shively distillery. For a bartender it is two lessons in one glass: bourbon need not come from a column still alone, and a bourbon can be built from more than one still.

records.table: Old Forester 86 Proof is the Louisville bourbon George Garvin Brown first sold in sealed bottles in 1870, the brand Brown-Forman was built on. Light and crisp at 86 proof, with orange, pear, mint and clove: a bourbon made for mixing.
records.story: George Garvin Brown (1846 to 1917), a young pharmaceutical salesman in Louisville, began selling Old Forester in 1870 with his half-brother. He sold it only in sealed glass bottles, as a guarantee against the watering and tampering of the middlemen who then sold whiskey from the barrel, and the brand calls it America's first bottled bourbon. In 1890 he went into partnership with his accountant and friend, and the firm took the name Brown-Forman. Through Prohibition the company held a licence to bottle whiskey for medicinal use, and by its own account Old Forester is the one bourbon sold by the same company before, during and after Prohibition. The first Old Forester went out at 90 proof; in 1959 the 86 Proof came in as a lighter bourbon for the cocktails of the day, beside the 100 proof that was kept. In 2018 the brand opened a distillery on West Main Street, on the Whiskey Row of its beginnings. For a bartender the 86 Proof carries the whole story of the sealed bottle in a bourbon light enough to mix.
